newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albanian PM works on crisis amid fresh warning.
newsitem.headline: Albanian PM works on crisis amid fresh warning.

text.p: Albanian Prime Minister Bashkim Fino was set on Monday to spearhead more efforts to solve a crisis over planned elections as Germany became the latest Western government to urge politicians to find a compromise.
The June 29 elections are vital to stop Albania retreating into the chaos of February and March after many lost their life savings in the collapse of crooked pyramid invesment schemes.
But most parties have threatened to boycott the vote unless changes are made to an election law which they say favours President Sali Berisha and his former ruling Democratic Party.
Fino's spokesman said the parties would meet again at 1100/0900 GMT to finalise suggestions on how to amend the law.
"After that Fino will meet Berisha to try and reach a final agreement on the law so that all the parties will take part in the elections," the spokesman said.
He added that Fino was unlikely to recall parliament to amend the law but would ask Berisha to use his presidential powers to issue decrees to amend it.

German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel was the latest Western leader to urge compromise in the crisis, following warnings from the European Union, Italy and the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE).
Kinkel in a telephone conversation with Fino late on Sunday urged the politicians to find a solution.
"This is in the interests of the Albanians and of the international community, which is committed to help Albania overcome the crisis," state-run news agency ATA quoted Kinkel as telling Fino.

Fino heads a nine-party government of National Reconciliation, including the Democrats, which Berisha was forced to install in March as anger over the collapse of the pyramid schemes boiled over into insurrection.
Most of the parties, including Fino's Socialist Party, want the election law to be changed to take control of the election away from Berisha and put in the hands of the government.
The row has dragged on as the parties, particularly the Socialists, remain deeply distrustful of Berisha.

The parties have issued an ultimatum to Berisha, which included demands for the government to name the electoral commission, changes in voting districts and a legal definition of the status of international monitors.
They also want the head of the Shik secret police and the head of the radio and television council, which controls electronic media, to be named within three days.
The parties want to make sure that the secret police are neutral in the elections and also prevent the single nationwide television station exclusively championing the Democrats.

The international community is anxious to make sure the vote goes ahead and avoid a repetition of the 1996 election, when the Socialists pulled out on the last day and which was called deeply flawed by the OSCE.
The election left the Democrats dominant in parliament but increased the other parties' suspicion that the Democrats want to hang to on to power at all costs.

European envoy Franz Vranitzky has warned that if a solution is not found then the OSCE and other international bodies will refuse to monitor the election, vital for them to be considered as free and fair in international eyes.
